question: The measurable quantity 'Density' may be represented in the SI unit of:
solution:
The correct answer is __**kilograms per cubic metre**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Density** is a fundamental physical property defined as the **mass** of a substance per **unit volume**. It indicates how tightly **matter** is packed together within a specific space.
 
• The mathematical formula to determine density is expressed as **Density = Mass / Volume**. This relationship shows that density is **directly proportional** to mass and **inversely proportional** to volume.
 
• In the **International System of Units (SI)**, **mass** is measured in **kilograms (kg)** and **length** is measured in **metres (m)**. Consequently, the unit for **volume** is derived as the **cubic metre (m³)**.
 
• By combining these base units, the **SI unit** for density is derived as **kilograms per cubic metre**, which is written symbolically as **kg/m³**.
 
• Density is considered an **intensive property**, meaning the value remains constant regardless of the **size** or **quantity** of the material being measured, provided the **temperature** and **pressure** are constant. ***Hence, the correct answer is kilograms per cubic metre.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **CGS Units**: In the **Centimetre-Gram-Second (CGS)** system, density is frequently expressed in **grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³)**. This unit is commonly used in **chemistry** and **laboratory** settings.
 
• **Conversion Factor**: It is important to note that **1 g/cm³** is equivalent to **1000 kg/m³**. For example, if a substance has a density of **2.5 g/cm³**, its SI value is **2500 kg/m³**.
 
• **Density of Water**: The **density of pure water** is a standard reference point, valued at **1000 kg/m³** (or **1 g/cm³**) at a temperature of **4 degrees Celsius**. This is the temperature where water reaches its maximum density.
 
• **Relative Density**: This quantity, also known as **Specific Gravity**, is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference material (usually **water**). Because it is a ratio, it is **dimensionless** and has **no units**.
 
• **Common Materials**: Different materials exhibit widely varying densities; for instance, **Air** has a very low density of approximately **1.2 kg/m³** at sea level, while **Iron** has a much higher density of about **7,874 kg/m³**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Effect of Temperature**: Generally, as the **temperature** of a substance increases, its particles move faster and spread apart, increasing the **volume** and thereby **decreasing the density**.
 
• **Effect of Pressure**: Increasing the **pressure** on a substance, particularly **gases**, forces the particles closer together. This reduction in volume leads to an **increase in density**.
 
• **Buoyancy and Floating**: According to **Archimedes' Principle**, an object will **float** if its density is **less than** the density of the liquid it is placed in, and it will **sink** if its density is **greater**.
 
• **Measuring Instruments**: Scientists use specific tools like **hydrometers** to measure the density of liquids and **pycnometers** to determine the density of solids or liquids with high precision.
 
• **Mercury**: This liquid metal is exceptionally dense, with a value of approximately **13,600 kg/m³**, making it much heavier than an equal volume of water.
